title: Personality is a feature
description: Products do not lose users to bugs half as often as they lose them to blandness. A case for designing character on purpose.
content:
Ask a team what their product feels like and you will get a roadmap. Ask their users and you will get an adjective. The gap between those two answers is where most redesigns should start.

Personality is not a coat of paint applied after the flows work. It is a set of decisions — how the product greets you, how it apologises, how loudly it celebrates, what it refuses to do. Those decisions get made whether or not a designer makes them. An unowned personality defaults to beige.

Character is a constraint

The useful move is to write the character down before the first screen. Two or three sentences: what this product would say at a party, what it would never say. Aura's was “a good host, not a butler” — warm, present, never hovering. That single line killed a dozen notification ideas in review, and every kill made the product more itself.

Constraints like this are cheap to write and expensive to skip. Without them, every contributor ships their own tone, and the product ends up with the personality of a committee.

The objection is always the same: personality polarises. Good. A product that nobody dislikes is a product nobody describes. You are not designing for everyone; you are designing so that someone, describing you at dinner, has something to say.

title: The case for slower interfaces
description: Speed is a virtue until it becomes a nervous tic. Sometimes the most confident thing an interface can do is take a beat.
content:
We optimised the wait out of everything, then wondered why nothing feels considered. There is a difference between an interface that is fast and one that is jumpy — and users feel it even when they cannot name it.

Watch someone sign a mortgage in an app that responds in eleven milliseconds. The speed reads as indifference. Some moments carry weight, and the interface should carry it with them.

Pace is information

A deliberate 400 milliseconds on a destructive confirmation is not latency, it is punctuation. The pause tells the user: this one matters. Stride's post-run summary fades in over half a second — not because we could not render it faster, but because arrival should feel like exhale, not interrupt.

The craft is in choosing where to spend slowness. Ninety-five percent of an interface should be instant. The remaining five percent — commitments, reveals, endings — earn their tempo. That contrast is what makes the fast parts feel fast.

Speed is table stakes. Rhythm is design.

title: Designing with defaults
description: The default state is the product. Everything else is a settings page most people will never open.
content:
Roughly nine in ten users never change a default. That number should terrify and liberate you in equal measure: terrify, because your defaults are your product for most people; liberate, because it means you get to decide what good looks like.

Teams treat settings as generosity. More often they are abdication — every toggle is a decision the team could not make, shipped to someone with less context to make it instead.

Defaults are opinions

The best defaults encode a point of view. Ledger ships with plain-language balances because we believe hex strings are for auditors. Verse opens with suggestions collapsed because we believe the writer's cursor is sacred. Users can change both. Almost nobody does — not because they cannot find the switch, but because the opinion is right.

A practical test for any new setting: if you cannot say which value ninety percent of users should want, you have not finished designing. The setting is a question you are asking your users. Answer it yourself first.

Strong defaults, few settings, and the humility to change the default when the data disagrees — that is the whole discipline.

title: Notes on taste
description: Taste is not a gift. It is a backlog of strong opinions you were willing to test against the world.
content:
People talk about taste like an inheritance — you have it or you do not. Ten years in, I think taste is closer to a savings account: small, regular deposits of attention, compounding.

Every designer I admire does the same unglamorous thing: they notice. They can tell you why a menu feels heavy, why a serif feels smug, why a green is cheap. Not because they memorised rules, but because they stopped scrolling long enough to ask the question.

Practising it

Three habits, none of them mystical. Collect ruthlessly — not moodboards of everything, but a small folder of work that makes you jealous. Copy privately — redraw the thing you admire until you can see the decisions inside it. And ship your opinion — taste that never survives contact with users is just preference.

The last one is the filter. Plenty of people have opinions about design. Taste is what remains after the world has edited them.
